question: During which period did the amount of ozone in the atmosphere begin to drop sharply?
solution:
The correct answer is In the __**1980s**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• This thinning of the ozone layer was particularly pronounced during the spring months (August-October) in the Southern Hemisphere.
 
• The phenomenon was termed the "ozone hole" due to the dramatic reduction in ozone concentration.
 
• Measurements from ground-based stations and satellite observations confirmed the rapid ozone depletion.
 
• The most significant and well-documented ozone hole is the one over Antarctica.
 
• Similar, though less severe, ozone depletion has also been observed over the Arctic region.
 
• The primary cause of this ozone depletion is the release of human-made chemicals, particularly chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs).
 
• CFCs were widely used in refrigerants, aerosols, and other industrial applications.
 
• When released into the atmosphere, CFCs drift up to the stratosphere.
 
• In the stratosphere, they are broken down by ultraviolet radiation, releasing chlorine atoms.
 
• Chlorine acts as a catalyst in the destruction of ozone molecules.
 
• A single chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules.
 
• This catalytic destruction of ozone leads to the thinning of the ozone layer.
 
• The ozone layer is crucial for absorbing harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the sun.
 
• Depletion of the ozone layer increases the amount of UV radiation reaching the Earth's surface.
 
• Increased UV radiation can have detrimental effects on human health, including increased risk of skin cancer and cataracts.
 
• It can also harm marine life and terrestrial ecosystems.
 
• The Montreal Protocol, an international treaty, was signed in 1987 to phase out the production and consumption of ozone-depleting substances like CFCs.
 
• Thanks to the Montreal Protocol, the ozone layer is slowly recovering.
 
• However, it is expected to take several decades for the ozone layer to fully recover to pre-1980 levels.
 
• Continued monitoring of the ozone layer is essential to ensure its long-term recovery.
